recipe.history:
The red bell pepper is the fully ripened version of the green bell pepper — the same Capsicum annuum fruit, simply allowed the additional weeks on the vine necessary to develop its full sugar content and its characteristic deep red color. The transformation from green to red is not merely cosmetic: during those extra weeks, the chlorophyll breaks down and is replaced by carotenoid pigments — capsanthin and capsorubin — that produce the vivid crimson color, while the starch converts to sugars, and the grassy, slightly bitter flavor of the unripe green pepper mellows into a rich, sweet, almost fruity complexity. Red bell peppers contain nearly three times the Vitamin C of their green counterparts and measurably higher concentrations of beta-carotene, making them one of the most nutritionally dense common vegetables. Capsicum peppers originated in what is now Bolivia and were domesticated throughout Central and South America over thousands of years before Spanish colonizers carried them back to Europe in the sixteenth century. They spread through southern Europe with remarkable speed — Spain, Portugal, Italy, Hungary, and the Balkans all developed distinct culinary traditions centered on the pepper within a century of its introduction — and from Europe they traveled with colonial trade routes to Africa, Asia, and the Middle East, becoming one of the most globally influential agricultural exchanges in history.

Roasted red pepper relish as a condiment belongs to the American culinary tradition of pickled and preserved vegetable accompaniments that stretches from New England chowchow to Southern corn relish to the Spanish-inflected pepper preparations of the American Southwest and California. The relish form — small-cut roasted peppers combined with vinegar, aromatics, and sometimes a touch of sweetness — was popularized as a gourmet burger and sandwich topping in American restaurants during the 1990s and 2000s, offering a more sophisticated alternative to raw sliced pepper while preserving the vegetable's sweetness and adding the complex smoky-charred notes of the roasting process. The Thin Red Pepper Burger draws on the aesthetic of the Thin Red Line — the military metaphor adapted to civilian life — suggesting precision, restraint, and an economy of means: one central ingredient, prepared superbly, doing the work that many lesser ingredients might crowd out.

I have an obsessive relationship with roasted red peppers that predates this recipe by at least a decade. It began when I spent a summer in Basque Country and ate pintxos made with piquillo peppers — small, sweet, smoky, and about a third the size of a standard red bell — roasted over wood coals and served simply with a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of sea salt on slices of toasted bread. The piquillo pepper is the distillate of everything a roasted red pepper can be: intensely concentrated, velvety in texture, sweet and smoky and faintly acidic in equal measure. I cannot always find them in my city, so when I make this relish with standard red bell peppers I roast them as aggressively as possible — charring the skin completely, steaming them long in a covered bowl, and letting them sit in their juices overnight in the refrigerator before I dress them. The overnight rest is the part most people skip, and it is the most important step. The flavors consolidate, the pepper softens further, and something almost wine-like develops in the juices.

The case for medium rare on this burger is a case for simplicity in service of truth. The Thin Red Pepper Burger is built around the singular, concentrated flavor of roasted red pepper relish — sweet, smoky, tangy — and the burger's other components are designed to provide context rather than competition. The beef patty at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) is the loudest voice in the composition: deeply savory, rich, and juicy. The roasted pepper relish is the next voice: sweet, smoky, bright. They are having a dialogue. If the beef is overcooked — dry, firm, flavorless without its lost fat — then the pepper relish has no one to talk to. It becomes a condiment on a filler, rather than a partner to a protagonist. Medium rare is the condition of that dialogue. It is what makes the simplicity of this burger mean something.
ingredients: 1 tbsp apple cider vinegar (for slight tang)
For the roasted red pepper relish:
2 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Freshly cracked black pepper, to taste
2 tbsp store-bought or homemade romesco sauce
4 slices Manchego or sharp cheddar cheese
1/4 small red onion, very thinly sliced
instructions: 1. Make the sourdough-style buns: Combine the warm water, sugar, and yeast and let bloom 5 minutes. Add the bread flour, salt, olive oil, and apple cider vinegar. Knead in a stand mixer with the dough hook for 8 to 9 minutes until smooth and slightly chewy — the apple cider vinegar adds a mild tang that mimics sourdough character. Rise in an oiled bowl for 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 equal portions, shape into tight rounds, proof on a parchment-lined baking sheet for 30 to 45 minutes. Brush with beaten egg and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake at 400°F (205°C) for 16 to 20 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

2. Roast the red peppers for the relish: Place the whole red bell peppers directly over a gas flame or under a broiler set to high. Char on all sides, turning with tongs, until completely blackened and blistered, 15 to 20 minutes. Transfer to a bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and steam 20 minutes. Peel away and discard all charred skin. Remove and discard stems, seeds, and ribs. Finely dice the roasted flesh into 1/4-inch pieces.

3. Finish the relish: Heat the olive oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Add the minced shallot and cook 3 to 4 minutes until softened. Add the minced garlic and cook 1 minute more. Remove from heat and cool slightly. In a bowl, combine the diced roasted pepper, cooked shallot and garlic, red wine vinegar, sugar, smoked paprika, red pepper flakes, parsley, salt, and black pepper. Stir to combine. Taste and adjust acid, salt, and heat. Ideally, cover and refrigerate overnight before using — the flavor improves dramatically.
4. Make the romesco aioli: Whisk together the mayonnaise, romesco sauce, sherry vinegar, smoked paprika, and salt until smooth and evenly tinted red-orange. Refrigerate until assembly.

5. Form the burger patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (8 oz / 227g each). Shape gently into patties approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick with a center dimple. Season both sides generously with salt and pepper immediately before cooking.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on the first side without moving. Flip once. Place a slice of Manchego or sharp cheddar on each patty. Cover the pan and add a splash of water for steam. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and the cheese is melted. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
7. Split the sourdough-style buns and toast cut-side down in the hot skillet for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

8. Assemble: Spread the romesco aioli on both bun halves. On the bottom bun, place a leaf of butter lettuce and a few rings of thinly sliced red onion. Place the cheese-topped patty over the onion. Spoon the roasted red pepper relish generously over the melted cheese, allowing it to cascade over the sides of the patty. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and a thin drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
